historical_timeline.summary: Born in Richmond, Virginia; the family moves to Missouri, and he is orphaned at about fourteen.
Joins William Ashley's fur-trapping expedition to the Rocky Mountains.
Struck in the back by two arrows in a fight with Blackfeet men; one iron arrowhead stays in his back.
Marcus Whitman removes the three-inch iron arrowhead at the Green River rendezvous.
Founds Fort Bridger with Louis Vasquez.
Marries his third wife, a Shoshone woman, after the deaths of his Flathead and Ute wives; several children.
Scouting for the Army; an officer's account notes that he cannot read but loves to be read to; a goiter troubles him.
Troubled by rheumatism and failing eyesight, returns to his farm near Westport, Missouri.
Eyesight fails rapidly; he recognizes friends only by their voices.
Almost totally blind; rides his farm on an old horse and walks his fields with a cane.
Dies on his farm near Westport at 77; reburied at Mount Washington Cemetery, Independence, Missouri, in 1904.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Low vision in an older man who works outdoors: a 70-year-old retired backcountry guide, who cannot read and takes in instructions by ear, comes in with two years of painless blurring in both eyes, glare and a fall. The episode covers the history and examination of gradual vision loss and its differential (cataract, glaucoma, age-related macular degeneration, diabetic retinopathy), with HbA1c, a dilated examination, intraocular pressure and macular OCT; the decision for surgery from functional impairment rather than an acuity cutoff; optical biometry, sequential phacoemulsification with lens implants in the worse eye first and the second eye six weeks later (with immediately sequential bilateral surgery discussed), postoperative drops and visits under the 1869 American Academy of Ophthalmology Cataract in the Adult Eye Preferred Practice Pattern; falls from low vision and from the mismatch between the eyes between operations; driving and the vision standard; chronic low back pain at the site of an old arrow wound, with an X-ray to look for a retained metal fragment (and before any MRI), and exercise therapy without opioids under the 1865 American College of Physicians guideline; a long-standing multinodular goiter with thyroid function and ultrasound under the 1863 American Thyroid Association guideline; knee osteoarthritis with exercise and topical diclofenac; and spoken, teach-back instructions for a patient who does not read.

assessment.assessment: Bilateral age-related nuclear cataract, dense on the right, fully explains the blurred vision, glare and faded colors, and the acuity matches the lens opacity. Glaucoma is excluded by normal pressures and healthy discs, macular degeneration by a normal fundus and macular OCT, and diabetic retinopathy by the absence of diabetes and of retinal signs

Surgery is indicated because the cataracts limit what he needs to do (faces, steps at dusk, driving) despite the best glasses; the decision rests on his loss of function, not on an acuity number. The right eye, the worse, goes first. The VF-14 questionnaire was not given today because it was not read aloud to him; his limits were documented by interview and the questionnaire will be read to him before the second eye

Phacoemulsification with a monofocal lens implant aimed at distance in each eye, from today's biometry; his corneas are regular and need no toric lens; glasses for near and fine distance afterwards. The left eye about six weeks after the right, once the first eye has healed and its result is known. Immediately sequential bilateral surgery on the same day is an option the AAO describes, with fewer trips and quicker recovery, but with the risks of a problem in both eyes at once; after discussion he chose separate days

assessment.assessment: Intracameral antibiotic at surgery, then moxifloxacin four times a day for a week and prednisolone acetate four times a day tapering over four weeks. Same-day contact for pain, redness or falling vision. Routine preoperative laboratory tests are not needed

His vision is below the driving standard now; no driving until it is met after surgery. Between the operations the two eyes will see very differently, which upsets depth judgment on steps; extra care, good light and handrails are needed, and the right lens of his glasses can be changed after the first operation to reduce the mismatch
